note — the bold part is what the card te: sein is irregular in every person, so learn its forms as a set: ich bin.
du bist: like most du forms it ends in -st, but sein changes its whole stem.
er, sie and es all take ist.
A noun as the subject takes the same form as er/sie/es: ist.
wir sind — the same form serves sie (they) and Sie (formal you).
ihr seid, with a d: not sind, which belongs to wir and sie.
sie (they) takes sind, like wir.
Formal Sie always takes sind, even when you speak to one person.

English: The man and the woman **are** here.
German: Der Mann und die Frau **sind** hier.
note — the bold part is what the card te: Two subjects joined by und are plural: sind.
ja stands outside the sentence, so the verb is still second: ich bin.
nein, like ja, does not count as a position: das Haus comes first, then ist.
ich is written lower-case unless it starts the sentence — unlike English I.
du is for one person you know well: a friend, family, a child.
sie with ist means she; the verb tells it apart from they.
wir: we.
ihr is du for several people at once.
sie with sind means they — only the verb shows it is not she.
Sie with a capital S is the polite you, for one person or several.
es stands for a das-word: das Buch → es.
der Mann is masculine. Always learn a noun together with its article.
die Frau is feminine.
das Kind is neuter: gender belongs to the word, not to the person.
der Hund: masculine.
die Katze: most nouns ending in -e are feminine.
das Haus: neuter. Das ist… points at anything — the second das is the article.
das Auto: nouns ending in -o are usually neuter.
das Buch: neuter.
der Tisch: masculine, though it is a thing — grammar, not meaning.
die Lampe: feminine, like most nouns in -e.
The subject takes the nominative: der Hund.
die Frau as the subject: nominative, unchanged.

English: The table is new. **It** is very big.
German: Der Tisch ist neu. **Er** ist sehr groß.
note — the bold part is what the card te: A der-word is er, even a thing: der Tisch → er.

English: The lamp is old. **It** is small.
German: Die Lampe ist alt. **Sie** ist klein.
note — the bold part is what the card te: A die-word is sie: die Lampe → sie.

English: The car is new. **It** is big.
German: Das Auto ist neu. **Es** ist groß.
note — the bold part is what the card te: A das-word is es: das Auto → es.

English: The dog is old. **He** is tired.
German: Der Hund ist alt. **Er** ist müde.
note — the bold part is what the card te: der Hund → er, as in English he for a pet.

English: The child is tired. **It** is small.
German: Das Kind ist müde. **Es** ist klein.
note — the bold part is what the card te: das Kind → es, whether the child is a boy or a girl.
